lead: A Thevenin source has a fixed open-circuit voltage V<sub>th</sub> and a fixed series resistance R<sub>th</sub>. Connect any load R<sub>L</sub> across its terminals. The power delivered to the load rises, reaches a peak, then falls as R<sub>L</sub> grows. The maximum power transfer theorem states that this peak occurs at R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>, and its value is P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>). The result guides impedance matching: audio amplifiers driving speakers, radio antennas feeding receivers, and sensor circuits passing weak signals to an amplifier. This chapter derives the peak and explains why maximum power is not maximum efficiency.
prereq: You need 2.4 Thevenin's and Norton's theorems to replace the fixed source by Vth and Rth.

blocks.text: Take the Thevenin equivalent of the fixed network: a voltage source V<sub>th</sub> in series with R<sub>th</sub>. Attach a load resistor R<sub>L</sub>. The same current I flows through both resistors, so I = V<sub>th</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>). The load power is P<sub>L</sub> = I² R<sub>L</sub>. Substitute I:

blocks.where: V<sub>th</sub> is the fixed Thevenin voltage in volts; R<sub>th</sub> is the fixed Thevenin resistance in ohms; R<sub>L</sub> is the load resistance in ohms; P<sub>L</sub> is the power delivered to the load in watts.

blocks.text: Two limits show the peak must lie between them. As R<sub>L</sub> → 0, P<sub>L</sub> → 0 because the load is a short circuit. As R<sub>L</sub> → ∞, P<sub>L</sub> → 0 because the current tends to zero. For finite positive R<sub>L</sub> the power is positive, so a maximum exists. The next section locates it. The figure uses V<sub>th</sub> = 12 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω; the peak is 9 W at R<sub>L</sub> = 4 Ω. The power produced by the source is P<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>); it is not the same as P<sub>L</sub>. This difference matters for efficiency.

Differentiate P<sub>L</sub> with respect to R<sub>L</sub>, holding V<sub>th</sub> and R<sub>th</sub> fixed. Write P<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>² R<sub>L</sub> (R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)⁻² and use the product rule.

blocks.where: dP<sub>L</sub>/dR<sub>L</sub> is the rate of change of load power with load resistance; all other symbols are as defined above.

blocks.text: Set the derivative to zero. The numerator must vanish: R<sub>th</sub> − R<sub>L</sub> = 0, so R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>. The derivative is positive when R<sub>L</sub> < R<sub>th</sub> and negative when R<sub>L</sub> > R<sub>th</sub>, so the point is a maximum. Substitute R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>:

blocks.where: P<sub>max</sub> is the largest load power in watts; V<sub>th</sub> is the Thevenin voltage in volts; R<sub>th</sub> is the Thevenin resistance in ohms.

blocks.text: At the peak the current is V<sub>th</sub>/(2R<sub>th</sub>), and the load power is (V<sub>th</sub>/(2R<sub>th</sub>))² R<sub>th</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>). The source resistance dissipates the same power as the load.

sections.h3: Maximum power is not maximum efficiency

blocks.text: Efficiency is the fraction of the source's generated power that reaches the load. The source produces Ps = Vth²/(Rth + RL). Therefore η = PL/Ps = RL/(Rth + RL). At RL = Rth, η = 0.5, that is 50%. Half the generated power is lost inside Rth. If RL is much larger than Rth, η approaches 100%, but PL becomes small because the current is small. The theorem answers one question: for a fixed Rth, which RL extracts the most power? It does not give the most efficient load or the largest load voltage. Use RL = Rth only when Rth is fixed and the source is a linear Thevenin equivalent. For AC circuits the condition becomes ZL = Zth*, the complex conjugate; see 2.7.

figure.caption: Load power for V<sub>th</sub> = 12 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω: it peaks at 9 W when R<sub>L</sub> = 4 Ω and falls on both sides. The marked point is the maximum-power operating point.

spec.aria: A plot of load power in watts against load resistance in ohms for a 12 V source with 4 Ω internal resistance, showing a peak of 9 W at 4 Ω.

examples.question: A DC network has a Thevenin equivalent with V<sub>th</sub> = 12 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω. Find the load resistance that receives maximum power and the maximum power itself. Also state the efficiency at that point.
steps: The source is fixed: V<sub>th</sub> = 12 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω.
Maximum power occurs when R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>, so R<sub>L</sub> = 4 Ω.
At this load the total series resistance is R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> = 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. The current is I = V<sub>th</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>) = 12/8 = 1.5 A.
The load power is P<sub>L</sub> = I² R<sub>L</sub> = (1.5)² × 4 = 2.25 × 4 = 9 W. Using the formula directly: P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) = 144/16 = 9 W.
The source generates P<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>th</sub> I = 12 × 1.5 = 18 W. Efficiency is η = P<sub>L</sub>/P<sub>s</sub> = 9/18 = 0.5 = 50%.
examples.answer: R<sub>L</sub> = 4 Ω gives maximum power, P<sub>max</sub> = 9 W, and the efficiency there is 50%.
examples.check:
Vth = 12
Rth = 4
RL = Rth
Pmax = Vth**2 // (4*Rth)
I = Vth / (Rth + RL)
Ps = Vth * I
eff_percent = 100 * Pmax / Ps
print(RL)
print(Pmax)
print(int(eff_percent))

traps: Saying maximum power occurs at maximum efficiency. At R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> the efficiency is only 50%.
Applying R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> when R<sub>th</sub> is not fixed or when the source is not a fixed Thevenin resistance.
Using P<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/R<sub>L</sub> instead of P<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>² R<sub>L</sub>/(R<sub>th</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)². The denominator must contain the total resistance.
In AC circuits, using R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> instead of the conjugate match Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>th</sub>*. The DC theorem alone is not enough.
Assuming the load receives all the source power at the maximum-power point. Half is lost in R<sub>th</sub>.

quiz.q: State the maximum power transfer theorem for a fixed DC Thevenin source.
quiz.a: For a fixed V<sub>th</sub> and fixed R<sub>th</sub>, the load receives maximum power when R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>, and that maximum is P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>).

quiz.q: Why does the load power fall to zero at both R<sub>L</sub> = 0 and R<sub>L</sub> → ∞?
quiz.a: At R<sub>L</sub> = 0 the load is a short circuit, so the load voltage and power are zero. As R<sub>L</sub> → ∞ the current tends to zero, so I²R<sub>L</sub> tends to zero.

quiz.q: A source has V<sub>th</sub> = 20 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 5 Ω. Find the load resistance for maximum power and the maximum power.
quiz.a: R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> = 5 Ω. P<sub>max</sub> = V<sub>th</sub>²/(4R<sub>th</sub>) = 400/(4 × 5) = 400/20 = 20 W.

quiz.q: A source has V<sub>th</sub> = 10 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 2 Ω. Compare the load power and efficiency at R<sub>L</sub> = 2 Ω and at R<sub>L</sub> = 8 Ω.
quiz.a: At R<sub>L</sub> = 2 Ω: I = 10/4 = 2.5 A, P<sub>L</sub> = 2.5² × 2 = 12.5 W, P<sub>s</sub> = 25 W, η = 50%. At R<sub>L</sub> = 8 Ω: I = 10/10 = 1 A, P<sub>L</sub> = 1² × 8 = 8 W, P<sub>s</sub> = 10 W, η = 80%. The larger load is more efficient but delivers less power.

quiz.q: For V<sub>th</sub> = 12 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 4 Ω, find the load power when R<sub>L</sub> = 8 Ω.
quiz.a: I = 12/(4 + 8) = 1 A. P<sub>L</sub> = I²R<sub>L</sub> = 1² × 8 = 8 W. This is less than the peak 9 W at R<sub>L</sub> = 4 Ω.

quiz.q: Does maximum power transfer mean maximum efficiency? Explain briefly.
quiz.a: No. At maximum power, R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub>, the efficiency is 50%. Half the generated power is lost in R<sub>th</sub>.

quiz.q: A fixed source has V<sub>th</sub> = 100 V and R<sub>th</sub> = 50 Ω. Compare R<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω and R<sub>L</sub> = 500 Ω for load power and efficiency.
quiz.a: At R<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω: I = 100/100 = 1 A, P<sub>L</sub> = 50 W, P<sub>s</sub> = 100 W, η = 50%. At R<sub>L</sub> = 500 Ω: I = 100/550 = 0.1818 A, P<sub>L</sub> = 16.53 W, P<sub>s</sub> = 18.18 W, η = 90.9%. The 500 Ω load is more efficient but receives less power.

beyond: Not for the exam. In radio design, conjugate matching transfers maximum signal power from an antenna to a receiver, and matching networks with inductors and capacitors transform one resistance into another. In low-noise amplifier design, the best noise match and the best power match can differ, so designers trade gain, noise and bandwidth. Power electronics usually seeks high efficiency rather than maximum power, so it deliberately avoids the R<sub>L</sub> = R<sub>th</sub> condition. Search for 'impedance matching', 'conjugate match', and 'maximum power transfer theorem AC'.
